Contents of https://www.bea.gov/news/2024/gross-domestic-product-fourth-quarter-and-year-2023-second-estimate:
**Real gross domestic product** (GDP) increased at an annual rate of 3.2 percent in the fourth quarter of 2023 (table 1), according to the "second" estimate released by the Bureau of Economic Analysis. In the third quarter, real GDP increased 4.9 percent.

The GDP estimate released today is based on more complete source data than were available for the "advance" estimate issued last month. In the advance estimate, the increase in real GDP was 3.3 percent. The update primarily reflected a downward revision to private inventory investment that was partly offset by upward revisions to state and local government spending and consumer spending (refer to "Updates to GDP").

The increase in **real GDP** reflected increases in consumer spending, exports, state and local government spending, nonresidential fixed investment, federal government spending, and residential fixed investment that were partly offset by a decrease in private inventory investment. Imports, which are a subtraction in the calculation of GDP, increased (table 2).

[![Real GDP: Percent change from preceding quarter](/sites/default/files/gdp4q23-2nd-chart-01.png)](/sites/default/files/gdp4q23-2nd-chart-01.png)

Compared to the third quarter of 2023, the deceleration in **real GDP** in the fourth quarter primarily reflected a downturn in private inventory investment and slowdowns in federal government spending, residential fixed investment, and consumer spending. Imports decelerated.

**Current‑dollar GDP** increased 4.9 percent at an annual rate, or $334.5 billion, in the fourth quarter to a level of $27.94 trillion, an upward revision of $5.8 billion from the previous estimate (tables 1 and 3). More information on the source data that underlie the estimates is available in the "[Key Source Data and Assumptions](https://www.bea.gov/sites/default/files/2024-02/gdpkeysource-4q23-2nd.xlsx)" file on BEA's website.

The **price index for gross domestic purchases** increased 1.9 percent in the fourth quarter, the same as in the previous estimate. The **personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index** increased 1.8 percent, an upward revision of 0.1 percentage point. Excluding food and energy prices, the PCE price index increased 2.1 percent, an upward revision of 0.1 percentage point.

**Personal Income**

**Current-dollar personal income** increased $219.5 billion in the fourth quarter, a downward revision of $5.4 billion from the previous estimate. The increase primarily reflected increases in compensation, personal income receipts on assets, and proprietors' income that were partly offset by a decrease in personal current transfer receipts (table 8).

**Disposable personal income** increased $202.5 billion, or 4.0 percent, in the fourth quarter, a downward revision of $9.2 billion from the previous estimate. **Real disposable personal income** increased 2.2 percent, a downward revision of 0.3 percentage point.

# Research Note — Lens 5B.10 (Joe Biden, 2023)

**Lens 5B.10:** Did the ruler leave the economy on a stronger trajectory than they inherited, accounting for external constraints?

**Inherited baseline (Jan 2021):** Real GDP –2.2% in 2020 (COVID), CPI inflation 1.4%, unemployment 6.3%, debt/GDP ~127% (post-pandemic surge). External conditions: ongoing pandemic recovery, fragile supply chains, monetary/fiscal stimulus overhang.

**End-of-2023 baseline:** Real GDP +2.5% (BEA second estimate, 2023 annual), CPI inflation 3.4% YoY (December 2023), unemployment 3.7%, gross federal debt/GDP ~118.6% (FRED). External shocks managed: SVB banking crisis (March), debt-ceiling standoff (May–June), ongoing Ukraine war, Oct 7 Israel-Hamas spillover.

---

## Favorable Evidence (trajectory stronger than inherited)

1. **Real GDP growth accelerated: +2.5% in 2023 vs. +1.9% in 2022, and far above the –3.4% contraction inherited from 2020.** (BEA, "Gross Domestic Product, Fourth Quarter and Year 2023 (Second Estimate)," Feb 28, 2024) — https://www.bea.gov/news/2024/gross-domestic-product-fourth-quarter-and-year-2023-second-estimate. Sustained post-pandemic recovery and resilience of consumption, exports, and nonresidential investment. *Maps to 5B.10; also 5B.1 sustainable prosperity.*

2. **Unemployment rate remained under 4% throughout 2023, ending at 3.7% in December 2023 — down from 6.3% at inauguration.** (BLS, "Unemployment rate inches up during 2023, labor force participation rises," 2024) — https://www.bls.gov/opub/mlr/2024/article/unemployment-rate-inches-up-during-2023-labor-force-participation-rises.htm. Tight labor market with rising participation. *Maps to 5B.10; also 5B.8 broad-based gains.*

3. **12.1 million jobs created since Jan 2021; Biden claimed "more jobs in two years than any president has created in a four-year term."** (PBS NewsHour, Apr 25, 2023; TIME SOTU coverage Feb 7, 2023) — https://www.pbs.org/newshour/amp/show/biden-touts-accomplishments-and-vision-as-he-officially-launches-reelection-campaign ; https://time.com/6253735/state-of-the-union-biggest-moments-2023/. Strong employment data was the core pro-Biden economic talking point. *Maps to 5B.10; also 5B.6 honest communication.*

4. **Inflation decelerated sharply in 2023 — CPI peaked at 9.1% in June 2022 and fell to 3.4% by December 2023.** (U.S. BLS CPI release, December 2023) — https://www.dol.gov/newsroom/economicdata/cpi_01112024.pdf ; https://www.bls.gov/charts/consumer-price-index/consumer-price-index-by-category-line-chart.htm. Disinflation occurred without a hard landing. *Maps to 5B.10; also 5B.1 prosperity, 5B.4 competent Fed handling.*

5. **Fiscal Responsibility Act (signed Jun 3, 2023) suspended the debt ceiling through Jan 1, 2025 — avoided default and capped non-defense discretionary spending.** (Wikipedia, "Presidency of Joe Biden," and Miller Center) — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Joe_Biden ; https://millercenter.org/president/biden/key-events. Bipartisan compromise preserved macro-fiscal stability despite extreme House GOP pressure. *Maps to 5B.10; also 5B.7 fiscal discipline.*

6. **Inflation Reduction Act ($369B for climate/clean-energy) and CHIPS and Science Act ($52B for semiconductors) drove major private-sector investment in 2023.** (Wikipedia, "Presidency of Joe Biden") — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Joe_Biden. Industrial-policy reorientation with bipartisan strategic logic. *Maps to 5B.10; also 5B.4 competence, 5B.1 sustainable prosperity.*

7. **Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act ($1.2T over 5 years) implementation accelerated in 2023.** (Wikipedia, "Presidency of Joe Biden") — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Joe_Biden. Long-cycle supply-side investments in roads, bridges, rail, broadband, EV charging. *Maps to 5B.10; also 5B.1 prosperity.*

8. **Federal Reserve independence preserved: Powell retained; the Fed raised rates from near-zero to ~5.25–5.5% by mid-2023 to combat inflation.** (Wikipedia, "Jerome Powell") — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jerome_Powell. Evidence-based monetary policy; Fed credibility preserved disinflation credibility. *Maps to 5B.10; also 5B.4 appointed competent professionals.*

9. **CHIPS Act 2023 implementation produced projects across multiple states (Intel OH, TSMC AZ, Samsung TX, Micron NY/ID).** (Wikipedia, "Presidency of Joe Biden") — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Joe_Biden. Broad geographic distribution of investment, reducing supply-chain dependence on Taiwan. *Maps to 5B.10; also 5B.8 broad-based gains, 5B.1 sustainable prosperity.*

10. **Operation Prosperity Guardian launched Dec 18, 2023 (12+ country coalition) to defend Red Sea shipping against Houthi attacks.** (Wikipedia, "Red Sea crisis") — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Sea_crisis. Protected global supply chains and trade routes — direct economic-trajectory benefit. *Maps to 5B.10; also 5B.9 managed shocks.*

11. **AUKUS "optimal pathway" announced March 13, 2023 (San Diego), committing the U.S. to sell Virginia-class SSNs to Australia — strategic and industrial investment.** (Wikipedia, "AUKUS") — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AUKUS. Long-horizon allied industrial capacity. *Maps to 5B.10 (industrial base); also 5B.9 managed shocks.*

## Unfavorable Evidence (trajectory weaker than ideal; headwinds and constraints)

12. **Inflation peaked at 9.1% (June 2022) before Biden took primary blame, and remained elevated at 3.4% by end-2023 — well above the 2% Fed target.** (U.S. Inflation Calculator historical data) — https://www.usinflationcalculator.com/inflation/current-inflation-rates/. The inherited pandemic-disruption inflation significantly eroded real wages, even as nominal wages rose. *Maps to 5B.10; also 5B.1 prosperity (constraint context).*

13. **Gallup Economic Confidence Index ended 2023 at –32 (up from –40 but still negative); 68% of Americans said the economy was getting worse.** (Gallup News, Dec 22, 2023) — https://news.gallup.com/poll/547763/biden-ends-2023-job-approval.aspx. Perception–data divergence persisted; inflation experience dominated sentiment. *Maps to 5B.10; also 5B.8 broad-based gains (criterion mismatch).*

14. **Federal debt held by the public remained elevated: gross federal debt/GDP was ~118.6% in FY2023 (FRED), little-changed from 119.6% in FY2021.** (FRED GFDEGDQ188S) — https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/GFDEGDQ188S ; https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/GFDGDPA188S. Despite "fiscal responsibility" legislation, the ratio barely moved — interest costs rising. *Maps to 5B.10 (sustainability question); also 5B.7 fiscal discipline.*

15. **Biden's third-year approval was 39.8% — the second-lowest of any first-term elected president in the modern Gallup era (only Carter's 37.4% lower).** (Gallup News, Jan 25, 2024) — https://news.gallup.com/poll/609188/biden-third-year-job-approval-average-second-worst.aspx. Partisan polarization 78 points (83% D vs. 6% R). *Maps to 5B.10 (governance constraint); also 5B.4 management of polarization.*

16. **March 2023 SVB / Signature / Credit Suisse banking turmoil forced emergency Fed/Treasury interventions (BTFP, implicit deposit guarantees).** (CFR, Kupchan) — https://www.cfr.org/articles/bidens-legacy-major-accomplishments-unfinished-business. Stress-tested financial stability; managed without broader contagion but revealed mid-tier bank fragility. *Maps to 5B.10; also 5B.9 crisis management.*

17. **No JCPOA revival in 2023; Iran advanced to 60% U-235 enrichment and restricted IAEA inspections.** (Wikipedia, "Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action") — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joint_Comprehensive_Plan_of_Action. Energy-market and non-proliferation headwinds unresolved. *Maps to 5B.10 (external constraint).*

18. **Oct 7 Hamas attack and subsequent Gaza war created energy-market volatility (oil price spike risk) and Red Sea shipping disruption beginning October 2023.** (Wikipedia, "Red Sea crisis") — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Sea_crisis. External supply-side shock late in the year. *Maps to 5B.10; also 5B.9 managed shocks (constraint).*

19. **Extreme partisan polarization (78-point Dem–Rep gap on approval) constrained the administration's ability to legislate after the 118th Congress's narrow GOP House majority.** (Gallup News, Jan 25, 2024) — https://news.gallup.com/poll/609188/biden-third-year-job-approval-average-second-worst.aspx. Governance capacity was structurally weakened. *Maps to 5B.10.*

## Mixed / Contextual Evidence

20. **Sentinel ICBM (~81% over budget in 2023 estimates) and broader defense-procurement concentration in five major contractors represent structural long-run costs.** (Wikipedia, "Lockheed Martin") — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockheed_Martin. Industrial-base costs and a fiscal drag in the longer run. *Maps to 5B.10 (mixed industrial-policy effects).*

21. **Russia's Feb 21, 2023 suspension of New START removed remaining U.S.–Russia strategic-arms transparency but the U.S. maintained numerical-limits compliance and avoided retaliatory escalation.** (Wikipedia, "New START") — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_START. Geopolitical headwind managed responsibly; no domestic-trajectory effect directly. *Maps to 5B.10 (external constraint context).*

## Net Assessment

**Favorable.** Compared to the inherited baseline (pandemic-contraction economy, 6.3% unemployment, elevated inflation running up from 1.4% to a 9.1% peak, ~127% debt/GDP, fragile supply chains), by end of 2023 Biden had steered the U.S. economy onto a stronger trajectory on the dimensions most directly under executive control: real GDP growth accelerated from 1.9% to 2.5%; unemployment fell to 3.7%; the disinflation path was credible without recession; the debt ceiling was resolved through bipartisan compromise; a structural industrial-policy triad (CHIPS + IRA + BIL) was operationalized with broad regional distribution; and the Federal Reserve retained independence.

However, three structural headwinds constrained outcomes and are essential to a fair read of "accounting for external constraints": (i) the inflation spike from 2021–2022 reflected largely inherited global supply-side shocks (pandemic recovery, war in Ukraine) and produced severe real-wage erosion that public opinion continued to register negatively through end-2023; (ii) federal debt/GDP barely declined from the pandemic-era peak, leaving the fiscal position roughly as constrained as Biden entered office; (iii) extreme partisan polarization constrained governance capacity and helps explain why second-rank legislative achievements (e.g., work requirements, IRS clawback) emerged from the debt-ceiling deal.

On balance, the trajectory of macro output, employment, and disinflation was stronger than inherited; the fiscal-stock trajectory was essentially flat; and the geopolitical/inflationary shocks of 2022–2023 spilled into 2023 perception data. The honest reading is **favorable on flows (GDP, jobs, inflation), neutral on stocks (debt, productivity), and unfavorable on citizen experience (real wages, confidence)**.

## Search-Gap Note

I conducted four targeted web searches (BEA, BLS, IMF/FRED debt-GDP, unemployment) plus two focused fetches. I was unable in this session to pull the following data points and they are noted as gaps if needed for downstream scoring:

- Direct BLS press-release confirmation of December 2023 nonfarm-payrolls print (BLS site returned 403 on direct fetch, but the BLS Monthly Labor Review summary and third-party rundowns both confirm 3.7% unemployment and ~2.0–2.3M jobs added in 2023 overall, consistent with the index).
- Precise 2023 real-wage (or "real disposable income") growth percent (BEA confirms real DPI +2.2% Q4; full-year average would need another query).
- S&P 500 / Nasdaq total return for calendar 2023 (widely reported as ~+24% S&P and ~+43% Nasdaq; not pulled here but consistent with index mentions).
- Manufacturing PMI / ISM full-year 2023 average.

These gaps do not change the qualitative net assessment but would tighten quantitative directional claims in a downstream rubric.
